summary:
North Dakota stands under the United States national framework in every respect that governs a trans visitor's documents, screening and entry. Executive Order 14168, in force since January 2025, requires federal identity documents to reflect sex assigned at birth; the State Department has stopped processing the X marker and any marker inconsistent with sex assigned at birth, issues new passports only as M or F on the supporting documents submitted, and leaves previously issued X-marker passports valid until expiry. Trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application, the ACLU has sued the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs, Lambda Legal maintains guidance on how name and gender changes interact with federal records, and the Supreme Court has allowed the State Department to proceed with its changed treatment of trans passports.

Entry carries a separate exposure. Executive Order 14201 of 5 February 2025 was followed on 25 February 2025 by a State Department announcement that trans athletes seeking to enter the United States to compete in women's sporting events will be refused visas and flagged internally under the code 'SWS25', and that an applicant declaring a gender other than sex assigned at birth may be treated as fraud and barred permanently. Airport screening adds involuntary disclosure: the National Center for Transgender Equality's know-your-rights guide describes secondary screening, body scanners and pat-downs as procedures that can expose a traveller's trans status to TSA officers and other passengers, and sets out how to request screening matching one's presentation.

North Dakota's own statute restricts identity documents sharply. The Movement Advancement Project's identity-document tracker records that North Dakota's 2023 law bans all gender-marker changes on birth certificates, with a narrow exception for individuals who have had genital surgery, and describes this as a stricter and more explicit surgical requirement than in many other states; the project marks North Dakota a 'negative law' state. The practical effect on a trans person who must show documents is that the birth certificate cannot be corrected, so presenting it outs them.

Erin Reed's anti-trans legal-risk assessment of 13 July 2026, built from five years of daily legislative tracking, lists North Dakota among the worst states for legislation targeting transgender adults and among the states that prohibit any changes to birth certificates. The same assessment records that federal policies continue to create legal difficulties for transgender people nationwide.

The state has also legislated directly against trans people in schools. House Bill 1522 of the 2023 regular session created sections of the North Dakota Century Code relating to preferred pronouns and providing accommodations to a transgender student, with a penalty provision and an emergency clause; the governor signed it and the final official action was filed with the Secretary of State on May 9, 2023. The statute is evidence of an official posture that a trans visitor will meet in a state that treats preferred pronouns and student accommodations as a matter for penalty-backed regulation.
tangentialFactors:
Restriction is a multi-state pattern rather than a North Dakota peculiarity. State bathroom bans applying to trans people in K-12 schools and some government buildings are in force in nine states and one territory, with additional states imposing outright bans on facility use by gender identity, and in some jurisdictions trans bathroom use is a criminal offence in certain circumstances; twenty-nine states, four territories and the District of Columbia have no such ban.

Enforcement of such laws has moved beyond statute. In April 2025 a trans student who announced 'I am here to break the law' and used a women's restroom at a state capitol building was arrested and handcuffed, in what civil-rights attorneys identified as the first known arrest under a state bathroom-restriction law.

One state's document statute is described by rights groups as a template other legislatures are following: a law invalidating birth certificates and driver's licences that do not bear sex assigned at birth and barring trans residents from changing those markers, with further targeting bills pending. The Movement Advancement Project's identity-document map sets out state by state which jurisdictions permit gender-marker changes on licences and birth certificates and under what conditions, so the rules a visitor encounters vary substantially across state lines.

Foreign governments have responded publicly to the federal document and data rules. At least eight European countries, including Finland and Denmark, adjusted travel guidelines for trans and nonbinary citizens entering the United States, advisories that followed detentions of European citizens over visa issues.

The July 2026 assessment designates four states do-not-travel for trans people, with a northern plains state most recently flagged on 13 July 2026, and records that the 2026 legislative season continued to degrade trans rights alongside the federal measures driving nationwide trends.
localsOnly:
North Dakota's 2023 statute bans all gender-marker changes on birth certificates, with a narrow exception for individuals who have undergone genital surgery. The Movement Advancement Project classifies this as a stricter, more explicit surgical requirement than many other states impose and marks North Dakota a 'negative law' state on its identity-document tracker. A resident whose birth certificate bears a marker inconsistent with their gender therefore has no administrative route to correction short of that surgery.

House Bill 1522 of the 2023 regular session, enacted as new sections of the North Dakota Century Code, relates to preferred pronouns and provides accommodations to a transgender student, carries a penalty provision and an emergency clause, and was signed by the governor with the final action filed with the Secretary of State on May 9, 2023. It is the state's enacted 2023 transgender-student statute.

Erin Reed's legal-risk assessment of 13 July 2026 places North Dakota among the worst states for legislation targeting transgender adults and among states prohibiting any birth-certificate changes, on a methodology drawn from five years of daily legislative tracking and a rubric for the worst bills; a regional LGBTQ outlet republished the assessment on 27 August 2026.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the current inventory documents a North Dakota statute governing access to sex-segregated facilities such as bathrooms or locker rooms, so the state's position on facility use is unresolved here. The nine-state tally of facility bans and the twenty-nine states without one are national figures that do not identify North Dakota either way.

Rules for changing the gender marker on a North Dakota driver's licence are not sourced in this inventory. The Movement Advancement Project maintains a state-by-state licence tracker that would settle the question, but no North Dakota licence finding is included in the material reviewed.

Whether North Dakota appears on the four-state do-not-travel designation recorded in the July 2026 assessment is not stated; only the most recent addition to that list is named. The inventory also provides no enforcement data on the penalty provision of House Bill 1522, no reported prosecutions or disciplinary actions under it, and no source on hate-crime or non-discrimination protection covering gender identity in the state.

The interaction between the state's birth-certificate rule and federal document processing under Executive Order 14168 for a visitor who holds an out-of-state or foreign birth certificate is not addressed by any source reviewed.
